MercadoLibre (MELI) stock looks increasingly attractive to me as political tension in Brazil weighs on sentiment. The e-commerce and fintech giant has seen its shares get beaten down lately. Brazil's post-election jitters compounded the pressure from the broader growth-stock sell-off.

Yet CFO Martín de los Santos reminded us of the company's strength. He said, "Users are buying more often and entrusting more of their money to Mercado Pago." Indeed, revenue grew 45%, despite disappointing earnings. I think that split explains the opportunity. Today's growth investment could produce much stronger earnings, while the decline has made MELI's valuation considerably more appealing, making me bullish on the stock.

MercadoLibre's Q3 Growth Remains Exceptional

MercadoLibre's Q3 growth was exceptional, in my opinion, despite the earnings miss. The report showed revenue and financial income rising 45% to $10.75 billion. Merchandise volume reached $22.8 billion, up 33% in constant currency. Total payment volume approached $109 billion, increasing 51% on that basis.

Unique buyers grew 22% to nearly 94 million, while fintech monthly active users rose 29% to about 93 million. Those figures show customers doing more across the platform.

Profitability was less impressive. Earnings per share (EPS) of $8.84 missed the $9.27 estimate, while operating margin fell to 6.3% from 9.8% last year. Fulfillment capacity expanded almost 20% sequentially ahead of peak season. New warehouses incur immediate fixed costs before order volume grows enough to fully utilize their fulfillment capacity.

Higher affiliate marketing spending also consumed margin. Basically, free shipping encourages smaller baskets, generating less revenue per shipment. Higher fuel costs added pressure, so the margin decline wasn't entirely discretionary. Still, I see substantial spending supporting future growth.

Brazil provides useful evidence. Revenue rose 50% in dollars, and commerce volume grew 36% in constant currency. Items per buyer increased 16% even after lapping the free-shipping change. This demonstrated that customers retained their new shopping habits.

The credit portfolio also grew 62% to $17.9 billion, while the share of loans 15–90 days overdue remained broadly stable at 7%. That is encouraging, although management is becoming more cautious in weaker credit segments.

Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre fell 9% last week after a third-quarter profit miss. Revenue rose 45%, but its operating margin fell to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier.

Most of the squeeze comes from loan-loss provisions and free shipping that management chose to pay for, so the margin should recover as growth slows.

Analysts expect earnings per share to dip to $37.45 in 2026 and then climb to $75.87 by 2028. The hosts of We Study Billionaires see a 13% to 14% operating margin by the end of the decade.

The main risk is a loan book that grew 75% in a year, because up-front provisions will keep weighing on the margin until that growth slows.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) sank 9% on a profit miss last week. Days later, the latest episode of the We Study Billionaires podcast came out under the title "We Doubled Down on Meli."

Growth wasn't the issue. Third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, while the operating margin fell to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier.

Shawn O'Malley was defending the growth forecasts in Daniel Mahncke's model on the episode when he reminded listeners that "Meli is the only company ever at significant size that was able to grow 30% or more for 30 consecutive quarters straight."

That's quite a streak. But the hosts' real bet is on where the margin goes from here.

The squeeze was on purpose

MercadoLibre's management hasn't been shy about why profits are down. On the third-quarter call, CEO Ariel Szarfsztejn said the company is investing because the opportunity is large and deeper engagement builds a lasting lead. Then he added: "We have accepted a lower margin to do that, and I think we've been open on that regard."

On the podcast, Mahncke broke down where that margin went. He called the provisions MercadoLibre books for its loans "actually the biggest part of the margin compression." He said that "in Q1, that alone cost four percentage points of operating margin," and two points in the second quarter. Next on his list was free shipping, which he called a response to Shopee in Brazil, and which he said has helped MercadoLibre outgrow its rival from a bigger base.

Then MercadoLibre added a logistics bill in the third quarter. CFO Martin de los Santos said on the call that the company grew its logistics capacity 20% from the second quarter ahead of the holiday peak, against 10% a year earlier. He expects part of that cost to come back in the fourth quarter.

title: MercadoLibre's Growth Strategy Puts Profit Margins to the Test

MercadoLibre's Growth Strategy Puts Profit Margins to the Test

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI is prioritizing customer engagement and marketplace expansion even as these investments weigh on margins. In the third quarter of 2026, net revenues and financial income increased 45% year over year to $10,750 million, yet operating income slipped 6% to $676 million. Operating margin declined 40 basis points sequentially to 6.3%, reflecting the cost of more free shipping, expanded fulfillment capacity ahead of peak season and increased affiliate marketing spending in Brazil.

Management identified a 60-basis-point sequential margin headwind from net shipping costs, including expenses associated with network expansion. Lower free-shipping thresholds encouraged customers to place smaller, more frequent orders, reducing revenue per shipment even as volumes increased. Higher energy prices added transportation costs, while fulfillment square footage expanded nearly 20% quarter over quarter ahead of peak demand. The expansion also brought temporary recruitment expenses. Meanwhile, sales and marketing spending rose 40 basis points sequentially to 11.6% of revenues as MercadoLibre stepped up affiliate investment in Brazil.

Despite these cost pressures, MercadoLibre reported measurable improvements in logistics efficiency. In Brazil, items sold increased 45% year over year, while cost per shipment fell 5% year over year in local currency and 14% from the first quarter of 2025 before the lower free-shipping threshold took effect. Management also reported that free & slow shipments in the R$19-R$79 price range in Brazil became variable contribution-positive as a group for the first time in September. Shipments per route reached a new high during the quarter.

These improvements show that MercadoLibre is working to lower delivery costs by handling more orders and improving efficiency. However, the company continues to balance the costs of expanding its shipping network and attracting customers against the efficiency gains from higher shipment volumes.

How Does MercadoLibre Stack Up Against Its Industry?

MercadoLibre, which competes with Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN and Sea Limited SE, has seen its shares tumble 17.2% over the past three months compared with the industry's 8.7% decline. While Amazon shares have fallen 6.7%, Sea Limited has plunged 34% in the aforementioned period.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) announced an FX-neutral revenue increase of 41% year over year alongside $676 million in operating income. Management sacrificed 40 basis points of operating margin to fund logistics capacity and affiliate marketing. Long-term investors need to know if these upfront spending choices build lasting competitive advantages. Three key takeaways from management explain how these capital choices position the business.

1. Logistics Expansion Sacrifices Short-Term Margin for Scale

MercadoLibre expanded its fulfillment footprint by nearly 20% in the third quarter ahead of the peak shopping season, incurring upfront costs before shipping volume arrived. Despite these short-term shipping headwinds, shipping cost per unit in Brazil dropped 5% year over year on an FX-neutral basis.

We added almost 20% to our fulfillment square meters quarter-on-quarter ahead of peak. That cost lands before the volume does, a pattern we have seen many times since we started operating fulfillment almost 10 years ago.
-- Martin de los Santos, Chief Financial Officer

2. Affiliate Marketing Investments Drive Social Commerce Acceleration

Management allocated extra capital to its social media creator network in Brazil, pushing sales and marketing expenses up 40 basis points sequentially to 11.6% of net revenue. The regional affiliate network surpassed 12 million members, expanding product discovery beyond traditional search channels.

Orders through the channel grew 240% year-on-year. Consumers increasingly discover and buy products through creators and social media.
-- Martin de los Santos, Chief Financial Officer

3. E-Commerce Customer Data Protects Credit Portfolio Performance

MercadoLibre expanded its credit portfolio 62% year over year while maintaining non-performing loans, or NPLs, aged 15 to 90 days at 7%. First-party shopping data from the marketplace allows the company to evaluate buyer risk before issuing credit lines.

And coming back to Brazil, I would say that an important advantage is that the marketplace gives us information before we lend. And we see how users buy, how they pay, how they use installments.
-- Osvaldo Gimenez, President of Fintech

Looking Ahead

Executive focus remains centered on artificial intelligence integration and proprietary ecosystem features. Internal development efforts prioritize in-house software capabilities over external platform integrations to safeguard customer relationships.

MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) delivered another round of strong top-line growth, but falling profits again sank the stock.

Shares fell 12% on Thursday as investors have grown impatient with the company's investment cycle, as it spends on lower free shipping thresholds, expanded logistics, and growing its credit business. However, that again led to narrower margins.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Revenue in the quarter jumped 45% to $10.75 billion, edging out estimates of $10.71 billion. Both core businesses delivered strong growth, with gross merchandise volume up 38% to $23 billion, and total payment volume jumped 53% to $109 billion.

Operating income in the quarter fell from $636 million to $601 million, and the company reported a net income margin of just 4.2%. On a per-share basis, earnings rose from $8.32 to $8.83 as the company benefited from lower tax expense. Still, that was below analyst estimates at $9.27.

MercadoLibre doesn't give guidance, so estimates are a bit of a guessing game, which works against the stock at times like these when it's investing in the business.

Image source: Getty Images.

Are its investments paying off?

The top-line metrics are clearly moving in the right direction, and management said it gained share in its three largest markets, Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina, which should quell concerns about competition from Amazon and Sea Limited's Shopee.

Importantly, the company continued to see engagement strengthening, and it sees a significant opportunity to grow purchase frequency, noting that its buyers make an average of 12 purchases a year, compared to more than 50 for e-commerce shoppers in developed countries. Faster shipping, lowering the free shipping threshold, and expanding its selection are part of its strategy to build a sticky habit and strengthen its competitive advantage, much like Amazon has done in the U.S.

The company is also seeing more customers adopt multiple products, which drive both revenue and margin improvement over the long run. As the business has scaled up, its cost per shipment in Brazil has fallen, down 5% in constant currency over the last year and 14% since the first quarter of 2025, a sign that it's effectively scaling its logistics operations.

Its credit card portfolio has been another source of headwinds on the bottom line, as the company needs to book a provision for expected losses when it issues new cards, even before it's earned any profits. The credit portfolio grew 62% to $18 billion in the quarter, and default and interest metrics remained stable.

Choosing between a established retail turnaround and a fast-growing international giant involves weighing local stability against global expansion. Investors must decide if Advance Auto Parts (NYSE:AAP) or MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) is the better buy today.

Advance Auto Parts serves the essential automotive repair market in North America, while MercadoLibre operates a massive digital ecosystem across Latin America. They are often compared because both rely on consumer health and logistical efficiency. Each company offers a different risk profile for those looking to diversify their holdings through 2027.

The case for Advance Auto Parts

Advance Auto Parts provides automotive replacement parts, accessories, and maintenance items to both professional installers and do-it-yourself customers. Professional sales, which include products sold to garages, service stations, and auto dealerships, account for nearly 50% of the company's total revenue. The business also supports hundreds of independently owned stores under the Carquest brand while operating thousands of its own retail locations.

In its latest annual report for FY 2025, revenue reached about $8.6 billion, representing a decrease of approximately 5.4% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of around $44.0 million, showing improvement over the previous year despite the decline in total sales. This focus on profitability is a key part of its strategy among retail stocks navigating a shifting economic environment.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 2.4x. This metric, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, means liabilities are more than twice the size of the equity base. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is approximately 1.7x. Free cash flow, representing the cash remaining after capital expenditures, was just about negative $298 million for the period.

The case for MercadoLibre

MercadoLibre operates a massive digital ecosystem that integrates e-commerce, logistics, and fintech services across 18 countries in Latin America. Its primary services include the Mercado Libre Marketplace, which relies heavily on third-party sellers, alongside the Mercado Pago fintech platform for various financial services. The company serves a diverse group of users, including individuals and small businesses that use its network for payments and shipping.

Based on its latest annual report for FY 2025, revenue reached roughly $28.9 billion. This reflected a significant growth rate of around 39% compared to the previous fiscal year. Net income for the period was about $2.0 billion, indicating that the business is successfully scaling its profitability as it expands its footprint across the region.

Shares of MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) fell by 12% on Nov. 5, the day after the company's third-quarter earnings came in below analysts' expectations. That leaves the stock more than 40% below its all-time high. Of course, some of it was due to broader market pressure, as the Nasdaq Composite had its worst day in years, but there were also numbers in the company's results that drove the decline. MercadoLibre is one of the largest investments in my own portfolio, so naturally, I'm not thrilled about the drop. But I'm not planning to sell a single share.

Another quarter of rapid growth

MercadoLibre's revenue grew 45% year over year to $10.75 billion, or 41% on a currency-neutral basis, slightly ahead of analysts' estimates. Its commerce business grew revenue 47%, and its fintech business grew 42%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

The underlying metrics were strong, too. Gross merchandise volume (GMV), the total value of goods sold on its marketplace, rose 33% on a currency-neutral basis. Total payment volume through Mercado Pago grew 53% to $109 billion, and the fintech platform now has about 93 million monthly active users, up 29% from a year ago.

So why did the stock fall?

In a nutshell, the problem was profitability. MercadoLibre earned $8.83 per share in the third quarter, below the roughly $9.30 analysts expected, and its operating margin shrank to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier.

Based on that, you might be wondering whether something is going wrong with the business, but I don't see any massive red flags. MercadoLibre increased its fulfillment capacity by almost 20% from the second quarter, offered free shipping on more orders, and increased marketing spending in Brazil. As CFO Martín de los Santos explained on the call, "The quarter when you are building capacity, you don't have the revenues yet, so you have the cost." He also said he expects margins to recover next quarter.

But the two biggest reasons MercadoLibre's operating margin fell year-over-year were higher operating costs and bad debts from the rapidly growing credit portfolio.

The lending business looks healthy

Speaking of the credit portfolio, it's also worth noting that side of the business held up. MercadoLibre's loan portfolio grew 62% to $17.9 billion, and the rate of loans 15 to 90 days past due was 7%, roughly unchanged from the prior quarter and close to historical lows, according to management. Management also said it's being a bit more conservative with new loans in Brazil and Argentina, which I like to see when a loan book is growing this quickly. There were higher rates of bad debt, but that's a function of the rapid growth of the credit portfolio, not of deteriorating credit quality.

The recommendations of Wall Street analysts are often relied on by investors when deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock. Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though?

Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about MercadoLibre (MELI).

MercadoLibre currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.42, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 20 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.42 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 20 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 15 are Strong Buy and one is Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 75% and 5% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for MELI
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for MELI

Check price target & stock forecast for MercadoLibre here>>>

The ABR suggests buying MercadoLibre, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.

In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

ABR Should Not Be Confused With Zacks Rank

Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether.

Broker recommendations are the sole basis for calculating the ABR, which is typically displayed in decimals (such as 1.28). The Zacks Rank, on the other hand, is a quantitative model designed to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

MercadoLibre stock was hit hard today. The shares dropped about 12% in regular trading, extending a weak run over the past month as investors reacted fast to fresh Q3 2026 numbers.

The headline result did not read like a collapse. Revenue reached about US$10.8b for the quarter and basic earnings per share landed near US$8.84. The real flashpoint sat in profitability. Trailing net profit margin sits at 4.9%, well below the 7.9% level from a year earlier and this matters far more for a business already trading around 41x trailing P/E.

Evaluating MercadoLibre's AI And Credit Margin Ambitions

Supporters argue MercadoLibre can keep funding heavy tech and lending build out while still protecting profitability.

"The main thing that has to go right is that management continues to balance heavy investment in logistics, AI and credit expansion with disciplined underwriting and controlled EBIT margins around current levels."

Q3 shows that tension clearly. Operating margin around 6.3% compressed slightly as free shipping, logistics capacity and Brazil affiliate spend all weighed on earnings, even while AI outlays rose. Credit volume and fintech activity stayed healthy with 15 to 90 day non performing loans at roughly 7%, which supports the underwriting side of the claim, but margin discipline is being stretched rather than reinforced.
